html:
Artifacts and output publication

agent_runtime/artifacts is production implementation, despite sharing a name with the repository's generated top-level output directory. The artifact store owns generated file identity, immutable versions, provenance and lifecycle. Collection registers actual files; previews, exports, download access and retention are separate responsibilities.

The output pipeline shapes actual results into display documents and exports. Publication does not manufacture execution evidence. A rendered table, chart or download card is a projection of an underlying result/version; completion still follows receipt and task contract validation.

For user controls and download behavior, see Generated files and previews.

Ownership and publication flow

Result presentation

The artifact lifecycle described below is separate from converting a tool receipt into readable output. The current native path uses these owners:

Owner Responsibility
Native publication Project accepted response/outcome facts, redact tool data and add sections from the last eight retained results.
Native presentation Hide credential-control receipts, make a bounded top-level preview and adapt native Gmail envelopes.
Result shapes Represent text, command streams, records, files, aggregates and email results with source identity and count hints.
Shape adapters Select the first matching normalization rule by priority, then adapter ID.
Display primitives Describe compatible presentation choices and their parameter/policy hints.
Display documents Resolve plan sections into structured content, rows, column hints and source references.
Renderers Format supplied shapes as Markdown/text or delegate to the structured document builder.
flowchart LR R[Saved receipt and result] --> P[Publication redaction] P --> N[Native preview and envelope adaptation] N --> S[Ordered shape normalization] S --> D[Structured display sections] S --> M[Markdown renderer] D --> U[Client presentation] M --> U

result_sections deep-copies the supplied projection. It clips each top-level string to 12,000 characters and each top-level list to 100 entries, marking the result truncated when clipping occurs or the receipt is incomplete. This is not a recursive bound on nested dictionaries or message bodies. Credential-required and credential-rejected receipts remain in control/activity history rather than becoming result sections. Other non-success/non-completed statuses normalize as errors on this path.

The general normalizer can prefer a referenced result-store payload when a store is supplied, falling back to the preview after a lookup error. Native presentation passes the already projected preview without a result store. Specialized email and capability adapters precede generic keyed payloads. Most default adapters accept success; command-output and generic dictionary adapters also accept completed. Error/skipped results select the error adapter, and an unconditional text adapter is the final fallback. A dictionary with both message and command stream fields selects the earlier message rule. Normalization does not replay a tool, recount a mailbox or calculate an aggregate.

Display plans and primitive manifests describe presentation intent. Their redaction_policy, constraints, safety_policy and max_preview_rows values do not enforce themselves. The document builder expects caller-validated source references; it raises when references are absent or missing and does not check primitive compatibility. With no explicit sections it deduplicates operation/data aliases. raw_available becomes true only when allow_raw_access is true and a source advertises raw data; the flag does not authorize retrieval or prove that the data still exists. Native result sections leave raw access disabled.

Generic Markdown tables use requested columns or the first row's keys. They do not escape every cell delimiter, and generic JSON rendering has no independent byte or depth bound. Input projection and client rendering therefore remain separate responsibilities. Structured documents carry column choices, but their Markdown fallback rebuilds generic row shapes and does not preserve those choices or every specialized email presentation. Email preview/approval shapes describe workflow state; rendering them cannot approve or execute work.

Publication prepares expensive projections outside the conversation collector's cache lock, then checks the run before exposing the resulting runtime view caches. A closed, unshared run is rejected. A result-conversion exception goes through the control-failure handler and replaces result sections with the resulting response. That handler preserves already accepted completion or a settled manual pause while reporting degraded publication; presentation failure must not invent a different execution outcome. See the conversation lifecycle for deletion ownership.

CSV helper versus registered artifacts

The table export helper serializes supplied dictionary rows into CSV, preserving explicit column order or the first-seen union of keys. Nested lists/dictionaries become semicolon-separated text; this is a lossy export. CSV quoting handles delimiters but does not neutralize spreadsheet formulas. The returned privacy value is metadata, not content filtering.

write_csv_artifact chooses an explicit workspace, settings.workspace_root, or the current directory. Its output directory comes from an explicit argument, auto_artifact_dir, or outputs. It creates that directory and writes UTF-8 CSV with a sanitized prefix and a UTC timestamp accurate to one second. The helper does not enforce workspace containment, and identical prefixes within one second can overwrite a previous export. File errors propagate. Its return value contains path, row/column counts, size and privacy metadata; immutable artifact identity, collection and download authorization require the registry flow below.

The isolated output tests cover shape selection, count hints, command output, structured rendering and temporary CSV writes. Native pause tests exercise the publication failure path. These tests do not establish browser rendering behavior or validate arbitrary nested payload sizes.

Artifact collection

Owner Responsibility
Runtime adapter Bind run/conversation identity, negotiate the original Gateway workspace and validate remote chunk transfers.
Collector Track writers, terminal observations, saved targets, retry state and conservative producer attribution.
Registry facade Select active RAM or standalone SQL storage, register immutable versions and serve verified private streams.
RAM registry Publish metadata, grants, quotas, events and derived indexes without doing slow blob IO inside hub transactions.
Presentation Enrich display Markdown after completion validation; historical reads use stored bindings only.
HTTP access Enforce access and conversation scope, expose metadata/previews/downloads and explicit collection/retention controls.
Browser renderer Hydrate cards, cache metadata/data, open previews and display collection/retention state.
Maintenance Schedule protected retention work through the active cleanup owner or standalone SQL adapter.
flowchart LR A[Accepted run and original target] --> B[Track writer and baseline] B --> C[Observe terminal or uncertain receipt] C --> D{All writers settled?} D -->|no| E[Retain pending collection] D -->|yes| F[Snapshot and stage eligible output] F --> G[Transfer revision-bound bytes] G --> H[Hash and publish immutable version] H --> I[Scoped metadata, preview and download] H --> J[Display-only answer enrichment]

Collection is an independent outcome. A successful command can have pending attachments, and a stopped command can still have finalized output to collect. Retry collection reads saved targets and terminal evidence; it does not replay the command or start another model turn. Unknown job/effect state keeps writer ownership pending. A later Gateway selection cannot supply missing fields in an old target.

Writer admission and collection share a per-run thread/process lock. This lock is released while the tool executes, but held during collector snapshots/transfers. It is separate from the short RAM publication transaction. A single writer receives exact producer attribution only when baseline, changed bytes and saved terminal snapshot agree. Multiple writers, missing observations or later changed bytes use conservative run-reconciliation provenance. Losing a workspace file records that fact without deleting its already registered immutable version.

Registry and integrity boundaries

ArtifactStore selects MemoryArtifactStore when the native state owner has a hub. Active metadata lives in RAM and follows the Controller checkpoint/recovery protocol; standalone tooling retains SQL transactions. Blob bytes live in generated-artifacts beside the native store path. Registration stages bounded content, hashes and fsyncs it, then publishes its version identity. RAM staging/rename happens before the metadata transaction, which rechecks retirement, cleanup claims, cancellation, latest-version identity and quotas. Failed publication cleans its new file; crash leftovers remain maintenance work rather than usable registry entries.

Identical intact bytes at the latest logical path reuse their artifact identity. Changed bytes create a new immutable version. Damaged prior bytes are quarantined; an unavailable latest version is never silently replaced with an older one in an export. Automatic registration preserves sensitivity across versions, including deduplicated bytes. An explicit revision-checked metadata patch is a separate path that can change display name, sensitivity or retirement without rewriting bytes.

Downloads first copy an authorized available version to a private temporary stream and verify its recorded size and SHA-256. Headers are sent only after this succeeds. Read/copy/verification failure attempts to quarantine the version; a successful stream is closed by response iteration or background cleanup. A digest establishes recorded byte integrity, not whether the generated file is correct or trustworthy.

Default quotas are 64 MiB per file, 512 MiB and 200 versions per run, and 512 MiB per ZIP export. Environment defaults are read when the limits model is constructed; explicit configuration can override them. Nondeleted versions, including quarantined ones, consume run quota. Existing quota failures reject publication without truncating a file into a successful entry.

Authentication and scoped reads

Artifact API access is conversation-scoped and sits behind the portal login boundary. An authenticated portal owner can create artifact sessions and download files without a second password prompt. Explicit AOR_ARTIFACT_API_TOKEN credentials remain valid only on the existing artifact endpoints; they cannot authorize workspace APIs. The launcher no longer supplies a default token. Legacy artifact-session cookies alone do not grant portal access. Cross-origin rules and artifact scope checks remain enforced. Portal logout, expiration and credential reset revoke owner access to artifacts too.

The inner legacy session helper retains direct-loopback/bootstrap behavior for standalone callers, but it cannot bypass the outer portal middleware in the product. Active RAM recovery invalidates legacy artifact-session hashes; standalone SQL sessions retain their expiry records. These are separate from portal owner sessions. An artifact grant can permit a fork to read source-run files. It does not grant the source answer's attachment projection or permission to reconcile that owner's run.

Preview and export policy

Data previews are bounded and rendered as inert text/table cells; HTML viewers use a response-level sandbox and CSP rather than rewriting the original HTML. Inline scripts can run inside the isolated HTML view, while network fetches, external frames, forms and external resources are blocked. SVG uses image-only serving; PDF opens its native browser viewer with its separate response policy.

Preview Bound or behavior
PNG, JPEG, WebP, SVG Up to 16 MiB; SVG is not promoted into the application's DOM.
PDF Up to 32 MiB through the native viewer.
HTML Up to 8 MiB in the sandboxed viewer.
CSV Read a 64 KiB prefix; show at most 50 data rows, 32 columns and 1,024 characters per cell. Counts distinguish complete parsing from sampled input.
JSON/text/Markdown Read a 64 KiB prefix as text; JSON formatting stops beyond depth 64 or the output bound. Invalid/deep/truncated data retains an explicit notice.
Sensitive or unsupported content Download-only; preview controls are disabled.

Retention and cleanup can make old files unavailable; a prior download link is not an unlimited storage guarantee. Literal credentials may appear in generated content. Optional FILES redaction applies at the model/receipt consumer boundary; these authorized browser previews and downloads are not a model-redacted copy. Sensitive marking disables previews but still permits authorized original downloads and ZIPs.

export.py selects the highest version per logical path, validates safe relative archive names and disambiguates Unicode, case and file/directory collisions. It writes an allowlisted manifest alongside the files. Missing latest versions reject the whole ZIP. A conservative preflight adds metadata allowance to uncompressed sizes, and the writer independently enforces actual archive size. The private ZIP completes before streaming and rechecks run authorization; an export is not an execution receipt or a new approval to run tools.

Output discovery and retained source

The workspace boundary creates conversation/run directories using SHA-256 hashes of their identities. Those names prevent identities from becoming path components; caller authentication and run ownership are still required. Generated output goes in OF_RUN_ARTIFACT_DIR. Publishable temporary output has a separate OF_RUN_TEMP_DIR, with hashed activity/receipt subdirectories when requested. TMPDIR on POSIX, or TEMP and TMP on Windows, points to that activity temp directory, otherwise run temp. Explicit command assignments can override these defaults.

The layout depends on negotiated capability. Legacy temp publication uses the Gateway instance's temporary storage, with a published child under run scratch. Runs requesting artifact_tmp_mapping use sibling files, scratch and temp directories under the artifact workspace instead. Scratch is not a discovery root. Eligible regular files in publishable temp are candidates regardless of extension, after the collector's writer-settlement checks; the discovery filter alone cannot establish that a file is finished.

Gateway discovery, reads and staging

Discovery returns relative paths, sizes, modification times and stat revisions. It visits at most 20,000 entries and descends to depth 32, counting excluded entries toward the entry limit. Hidden names, editor/partial/lock/database files, internal directories, symlinks/reparse points and special files are excluded. POSIX traversal opens child directories relative to a held descriptor with O_NOFOLLOW; failed or over-limit scans raise an error rather than returning a complete-looking subset.

The artifact reader accepts safe workspace-relative names, including artifact-workspace:// names, or absolute paths already within that workspace. It rejects traversal and descendant aliases even when they point back inside the root. Opened files must be regular files, and Windows additionally verifies the opened handle's final path. Reads transfer at most 256 KiB per response, check an expected revision when supplied, and enforce the requested whole-file size limit, which defaults to 64 MiB. That request limit is separate from the Controller registry quota. Stat revisions detect identity/metadata changes; the Controller computes the content digest during registration.

Temporary-file staging copies a validated source to an exclusive private partial inside the destination. It holds destination directory handles, checks source revision and size, flushes the copy and verifies the opened source before atomic replacement. A known unchanged source and matching staged revision can reuse an earlier copy. Failure removes the partial; success supplies source and staged revision metadata for later transfer. Staging alone does not create a downloadable Controller artifact.

Explicit legacy system-temp references can be staged on the original Gateway; global temp is never crawled. Only trusted OS root aliases are resolved, while caller-controlled descendants retain no-follow checks. The instance-state root, reserved smto directories and the current run workspace are excluded from legacy fallback sources. The Server never opens a remote path locally. Older Gateways keep workspace collection and receive no unsupported temp actions.

Negotiated Linux /tmp routing

The Controller adapter requests mapping only when the accepted Gateway capability snapshot advertises artifact_tmp_mapping. The returned environment must explicitly report OF_RUN_TMP_MAPPING=1 or 0; capability advertisement does not prove that the host supports the mount. The Gateway supervisor probes bubblewrap and preservation of the original user namespace before executing a user command. Missing support, a failed five-second probe, or backing storage under /tmp selects managed TMPDIR fallback. Scratch markers preserve that downgrade across later calls and Gateway restarts; a concurrent downgrade wins over probe success.

When active, only the child mount maps /tmp to this run's temp directory. This retains the host filesystem view and is not a general execution sandbox. Working-directory resolution therefore defers mapped /tmp paths to the child instead of validating an unrelated host path. File argument translation uses the same run interpretation. Explicit/default working directories elsewhere retain their normal target-local semantics.

The launch supervisor records readiness immediately before the user command. It holds that receipt's inode open, so deleting the scratch filename cannot make an executed command appear unstarted. A ready receipt or signal termination prevents a fallback replay, regardless of the command's exit code. Only mount setup failure before execution can downgrade and run the command with managed TMPDIR. Invalid workspace identity is a hard failure rather than an optional mount failure. These rules are shared by shell, job, captured terminal, detached terminal and privilege launch adapters.

For mapped runs, an explicit /tmp/file reference always means the run's file; a missing run file never falls back to a same-named host file. Once downgraded, that alias is rejected for publication; the explicit managed temp path remains usable. This prevents earlier run references from being reinterpreted as unrelated shared-temp content.

Retained source and reference discovery

Executed terminal python.run attempts also retain their exact submitted UTF-8 source at source/python/<operation hash>.py, excluding wrappers and injected inputs. Shell command strings are not automatically stored as scripts. Files remain downloadable through the existing artifact surface after Gateway cleanup or disconnection. Images render inline from authorized server artifact endpoints; other files use the existing preview/download cards. Display enrichment happens after completion validation and adds zero model calls. Stored source bindings support deterministic retries and history rendering without resolving old paths against a newly selected Gateway.

Reference discovery in references.py is bounded to 64 unique paths, 262,144 inspected string characters, 2,048 visited values and depth 12. Execution inputs, diagnostic path fields and assistant fenced examples are excluded. Finding a path is only a publication candidate; the original target's staging and transfer checks still decide whether it is safe and available. Conflicting retained bindings from different targets are omitted from display enrichment. Plan responses retain their canonical digest-bound text.

Browser ownership and refresh

The shared renderer attaches one context to each response. Metadata/data requests share a four-request queue per context; run-list refreshes, image loads and downloads have separate lifetimes. Session POSTs are coalesced across contexts, and expired session responses get one renewal retry. Metadata failures can remain cached until a list refresh replaces them; failed data previews are evicted for an explicit retry.

Run centers build their tables when opened and refresh from server count/revision summaries or explicit artifact events. No artifact polling timer runs here. Late results cannot repaint disconnected/rebound references. Dialogs close when their response disappears, while already sent requests continue. The host owns the DOM; global artifact listeners are removed when a later artifact-change event observes detachment, rather than through an immediate destroy hook.

Retention and recovery

Conversation policy supports inherited conversation retention, 7/30/90-day expiry, or keeping files until explicit deletion. Age uses the last artifact update, not the last download. Native owners, uncertain receipts/jobs, queued follow-ups, unfinished collection, related tasks/schedules/monitors and retained grants/links can protect a namespace. Unknown native state is retained conservatively.

Active RAM maintenance prepares work through the save/cleanup coordinator, tying removal to recovery evidence and yielding between units for foreground execution. Fallback RAM cleanup uses per-namespace claims and does file IO outside hub callbacks. Standalone SQL cleanup retains its serialized transaction and can remove files before commit; a later SQL rollback cannot restore those bytes. Missing-file quarantine is part of recovery. Old orphan files/namespaces have a 24-hour grace, with safe path and ownership checks; this is not a scan of unrelated system temp.

Gateway startup attempts to clear unprotected artifact caches, then checks every 24 hours. Missing/offline job ownership evidence defers cleanup. The daily pass removes caches idle for at least 24 hours, including staged workspace files and publishable task temp. Active requests and tracked running or uncertain jobs protect their files. Private scratch, unrelated shared temp files and saved server artifacts are preserved. Output that has not reached the server can be lost at startup or expiry; server downloads continue to use their separate conversation retention policy. Cleanup is shared by all Gateway platforms and both connection modes, in gateway_core/artifact_maintenance.py. Its process-wide activity counter also protects wrapped streaming reads while they are consumed; it is not a cross-process execution lease.
